passage:
Sunday, 9:40 p.m. A small win to record. Last week, before the product launch got busy, I sent Seema, my manager, one message: "I will be offline after seven on weekdays, and I will need Friday afternoon off after Thursday's late push." Seema said fine and moved a meeting. So from Monday to Wednesday I switched the lights off by eleven, ate lunch away from the desk and took a twenty-minute walk after work. Thursday's push ran until nine and it went well. On Friday afternoon I did nothing at all, which felt strange and then good. Today I caught two mistakes in the slides that I would have missed if I had worked through the night. Note to self: rest is a step in the work, not a reward for it.
Jeevan

qa.q: After what time did Jeevan say weekdays would be offline?
qa.a: Jeevan said the weekdays would be offline after seven.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel about doing nothing on Friday afternoon?
qa.a: Jeevan felt uneasy at first, because doing nothing felt strange, and then content as the afternoon came to feel good.

qa.q: Why was it wise to state the limit before the launch got busy?
qa.a: It gave Seema time to move a meeting and plan around it, so it came as a plan and not as a complaint.

qa.q: How might Seema have felt on receiving that message?
qa.a: Probably cooperative and fine with it, since Seema agreed and moved a meeting, and may have valued the early notice. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a worker who protects sleep, meals, a walk and time off by stating limits early, and produces better work as a result.

passage:
Yamini: Are you up? Client wants the deck by 9 tomorrow 😬
Akash: I am signing off. Phone is charging in the other room.
Akash: I will take the deck at 7:30 with my tea. An hour of work, so it will be sent before nine.
Yamini: You could not just glance at it tonight?
Akash: A tired glance gives you a worse deck. And I told the team on Monday that my cut-off is ten.
Yamini: Fair. Fine. Sleep well.
(Next morning, 8:40)
Akash: Sent. Fixed three slides. Also found a wrong figure I would have missed last night.
Yamini: Client loved it. 🙂 I am going to bed early tonight too.
Akash: Good. Lunch together, away from our desks?
Yamini: Yes. And a walk after.

qa.q: By what time did Akash say the deck would be sent?
qa.a: Akash said it would be sent before nine, after starting at 7:30.

qa.q: What was Akash thinking when refusing a quick look that night?
qa.a: That a tired review would give a worse deck, and Akash felt calm and firm about the ten o'clock cut-off.

qa.q: What went right in the way Akash handled the request?
qa.a: Akash stated the cut-off, offered a specific early time and delivered, so the client got a better deck.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel after the client loved the deck?
qa.a: Relieved, and a little convinced, since Yamini decides to go to bed early too and agrees to lunch and a walk.

grounding: Illustrates a worker who states a sleep cut-off, delivers first thing next morning, and shows that a rested mind gives better work.

subtype: Reducing load rather than powering through [Response]
passage:

Gargi: Yes. Sent it at 9. "I am running low. Can I drop the vendor report this month and share Thursday's call with Reema?"

qa.q: Why was asking early a sensible choice?

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel watching Gargi ask for less?
qa.a: Concerned earlier, since Zeenat said Gargi looked wrecked, and now proud and reassuring. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a person feeling worn down who asks to drop and share tasks and books a doctor's visit for persistent headaches.

passage: Vidya had been marking notebooks at midnight for a month, teaching all day and keeping the mid-day meal register too. In the village school near Vellore, the bell was the only thing keeping her upright. On Wednesday she noticed she had read the same answer three times and had snapped at a child, which she hated. At lunch she went to the headmaster's room. "Sir, I cannot do everything properly. Could Abhinav keep the meal register until Diwali, and could I hand over the Saturday class this term?" Abhinav, who was drinking his tea in the doorway, said, "Give it to me, I have free periods." The headmaster nodded. That Saturday Vidya slept until seven, and on Monday she went to the health centre, because the tiredness had lasted so long.

qa.q: What did Vidya ask Abhinav to keep until Diwali?
qa.a: Vidya asked Abhinav to keep the mid-day meal register until Diwali.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling after snapping at a child?
qa.a: Guilty and worn out, since she hated having done it.

qa.q: What was the turning point that led Vidya to act?
qa.a: Noticing that she had read the same answer three times and snapped at a child; she then asked the headmaster to reduce her load and went to the health centre.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see Vidya's request?
qa.a: Probably as a sensible one and not a lack of commitment, since Abhinav offered to help at once because of free periods.

grounding: Illustrates a worn-down person who asks to hand over tasks early and goes to the health centre when the tiredness persists.

passage: Listen, beta, Ganga Nani is going to tell you something. When I was fourteen, my friend Damini joined the swimming class at the canal-side club. The first month was all fun. Then the coach began teaching the breathing turn, and Damini swallowed water twice and coughed for ten minutes. She stopped coming. "It is boring," she said, "just lap after lap." I noticed she never once said it was hard. The coach came to her house and offered to move her to the shallow group for two weeks. She said no. The next summer I swam across the canal with the others, and Damini stood on the bank holding towels. Years later she told me, "I left right before it got good."

qa.q: What did Damini say when she stopped coming to swimming class?
qa.a: Damini said, "It is boring, just lap after lap."

qa.q: What was Damini probably feeling when she swallowed water and then called class boring?
qa.a: Discouraged and uncomfortable, but she called it boredom and never said it was hard.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Damini have chosen differently?
qa.a: When the coach offered the shallow group for two weeks; accepting would have let her stay through the hard part.

qa.q: How might the coach have felt when Damini said no?
qa.a: Disappointed and concerned, having come to her house and offered a gentler way to keep going.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who leaves a class as soon as it becomes hard, calls it boredom and later regrets leaving before it got good.

passage: Rain hammered the tin roof of the school shed, and the district trial was two days away. Damini had missed three penalty saves in a row since the coach moved her to goalkeeper, and her gloves were soaked. "This is boring," she announced, dropping them by the bench. "I want to go home." Rukmini, holding the umbrella over both girls, stared at her. "You were not bored on Monday when you played striker." Damini shrugged and walked off toward the bus stop, where the bus was already late and packed. She counted her coins for the fare and thought about what she had said. On Thursday she did not turn up for the trial, and the team drew lots for a substitute keeper.

qa.q: How many penalty saves in a row had Damini missed?
qa.a: Damini had missed three penalty saves in a row.

qa.q: What was Damini really feeling when she called practice boring?
qa.a: Frustrated and discouraged by the missed saves, which she labelled as boredom.

qa.q: What could Damini try before deciding to leave?
qa.a: Ask the coach for extra keeper practice or a short break, and still go to the trial.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel as Damini walks off?
qa.a: Puzzled and worried, since Rukmini points out that Damini was not bored on Monday.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who drops a sport position at the first real difficulty and calls it boredom.

passage:
My roommate Bhavna has disliked her design diploma since the first term. She says so at night, quietly, with the lights off. But whenever I ask why she does not switch, she says, "I have already paid two years of fees and finished four semesters." She showed me the printed receipts in a folder tied with a rubber band, as if they were arguments. Last week she sat up until two rewriting a portfolio she called pointless. I cannot see inside her head, and maybe she is more hopeful than she lets on. But I noticed she talks about the fees more than the work. When a friend mentioned a coding bootcamp, Bhavna changed the subject and reached for the folder.
Tenzin

qa.q: What did Bhavna keep in a folder tied with a rubber band?
qa.a: Bhavna kept the printed receipts of her fees in the folder.

qa.q: What might Bhavna be feeling when she reaches for the folder?
qa.a: Anxious and stuck, unwilling to let go of the money and time already spent, though Tenzin cannot be certain.

qa.q: What question could help Bhavna decide about the diploma?
qa.a: Whether the coming semesters are worth it, because the fees already paid cannot be changed.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel when the idea of switching keeps being shut down?
qa.a: Frustrated and worried, but still willing to keep asking gently.

grounding: Illustrates a student who stays in a course that no longer fits because of what has already been paid and finished, seen by a roommate.

passage: On Saturday, Binita sat in a café while Tejas talked about the job he might take abroad without asking what she wanted, and she nodded, as she had for months. She thought, three years, I cannot waste them. On Wednesday she made a list for her sister of everything the two of them had done together, the trips and the birthdays, and could not write a single line about the coming year. On Sunday, on the bus, she asked herself a different question: if today were the first day, would I choose this? The answer came slowly, and it was no. It frightened her more than the list had. She decided to talk to Tejas after the weekend.

qa.q: What did Binita write for her sister on Wednesday?
qa.a: Binita made a list of everything she and Tejas had done together, the trips and the birthdays.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling on Saturday as she nodded at Tejas's plans?
qa.a: Small and unheard, yet reluctant to let three years go.

qa.q: What question helped Binita see things differently?
qa.a: She asked whether she would choose this relationship if today were the first day.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel when Binita talks to him?
qa.a: Probably surprised and hurt, since he may not have noticed how she felt while she kept nodding.

grounding: Illustrates a student who stays in a relationship because of years already invested even though it stopped fitting.

passage: In Santiago, Pablo stood in the hallway with his running shoes in his hand and thought about quitting. Six weeks of training, and his legs felt heavy and his times were worse. He phoned Nour, who coached the university running group. "Is it the race, the plan, or just a rough patch?" she asked. He thought about it. He still wanted the race. The plan was three hard runs a week with no rest, and his semester exams were this week. So he cut it to two easy runs, swapped one for a bike ride and wrote "review on the 20th" on the fridge whiteboard. On the 20th his legs felt lighter, and he chose to keep going.

qa.q: What did Pablo write on the fridge whiteboard?
qa.a: Pablo wrote "review on the 20th".

qa.q: How did Pablo feel once he thought about Nour's question?
qa.a: Pablo felt steadier and still determined, because he realised he still wanted the race, so the goal itself was not the problem.

qa.q: Why was the review date a useful step?
qa.a: It turned quitting into a considered choice, letting him try a lighter plan before deciding.

qa.q: How might Nour have felt about Pablo's call?
qa.a: Glad to help, and probably pleased that Pablo was checking the goal, the plan and the phase before quitting.

grounding: Illustrates a person who asks whether the goal, the method or a passing phase is the problem, adjusts the plan and sets a review date.

passage: In the college music room, Sachin put his guitar back in its case and said, "I think I should quit the band." Preeti, the band's secretary, kept writing in her register. "Is it the music, or the schedule?" "Rehearsal is at eight in the evening and my lab reports are due," Sachin said slowly. "It is the timing. And the fest month is a mess." Preeti suggested moving his slot to Sundays and taking the next two weeks off. They wrote the 14th on the notice board: "Sachin: review." Two weeks later, Sachin walked in with a new riff he had made on the train.

qa.q: What date was written on the notice board for Sachin's review?
qa.a: The 14th was written on the notice board.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling about the band when he said he should quit?
qa.a: Overwhelmed by the schedule pressure and not tired of the music itself.

qa.q: What options did Preeti offer instead of quitting?
qa.a: Moving his slot to Sundays, taking two weeks off and setting a review date.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel about a member leaving in the middle of the fest month?
qa.a: Concerned but supportive, since she asked about the cause before accepting the quit.

grounding: Illustrates a person who checks whether a schedule, not the activity, is the problem and pauses with a review date before quitting.

passage: It took me eleven weeks to write one email. Amma thought a stable firm was a gift, and I felt guilty just thinking about leaving. I listed my reasons on paper: the work no longer taught me anything, and I dreaded Mondays. I told Sunaina, my team lead, before anyone else, and "Nitin, are you sure?" was all she said. I gave six weeks' notice, wrote a handover document for each client and trained Arjun on the reports. I was afraid, and on the last Friday relief came first, then a lump in my throat as the team clapped. Guilt still surfaces when Amma asks about my plans, but I would rather remember that I left with the folders in order.

qa.q: How many weeks' notice did Nitin give?
qa.a: Nitin gave six weeks' notice.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Nitin have on the last Friday?
qa.a: Relief first, then a lump in the throat, on top of fear and lingering guilt about Amma's hopes.

qa.q: What steps made Nitin's leaving graceful?
qa.a: Telling the team lead first, giving six weeks' notice, writing handover documents and training Arjun.

qa.q: How might Amma see Nitin's decision?
qa.a: Probably with worry about security, since Nitin says Amma thought a stable firm was a gift.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional who feels guilt, fear and relief about leaving and handles reasons, timing and handover carefully.

passage: Supervisor's note, Sudha. Sachin asked to speak after the field team left today. He said he wanted to leave the survey project by the end of April, and he apologised three times in five minutes. He looked relieved to have said it and then scared. He told me his parents expected him to hold a steady job and that he did not want to let the team down. I asked what he wanted to happen before he goes. He proposed finishing the two remaining districts, writing the data-entry guide and training Neha to take over. I agreed the end date in writing, told the director the same day, and set a weekly check-in until the handover is done. I also told him his reasons sounded well thought through.

qa.q: How many times did Sachin apologise in five minutes?
qa.a: Sachin apologised three times in five minutes.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling once he had said he wanted to leave?
qa.a: Relieved, then scared, and guilty about letting the team down.

qa.q: What could Sachin do in the weeks before leaving?
qa.a: Finish the two districts, write the data-entry guide and train Neha, with weekly check-ins.

qa.q: How does Sudha see Sachin's decision?
qa.a: As well thought through and worth supporting with a written end date and check-ins.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional leaving a project with guilt and fear about family expectations and colleagues, and planning a careful handover.

passage: Counsellor's note, Bidisha. Gurleen came in on Tuesday after a tense dinner. She wants to leave her accounting articleship for a design course, and her parents said, "You will waste four years and come back with nothing." She was shaking with anger at first. On Thursday she returned with a one-page plan: the course fee, six months of savings, an idea for weekend part-time work, and a date to decide again if her portfolio brings no interviews. We rehearsed a calm opening line about her parents' worry for her security. On Saturday she read it to them. Her father stayed silent, and her mother asked to keep the page. I asked Gurleen to keep listening rather than argue, and offered to meet her parents if they wish.

qa.q: What did Gurleen bring back on Thursday?
qa.a: Gurleen brought a one-page plan with the course fee, savings, a part-time work idea and a date to decide again.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling after the tense dinner?
qa.a: Anger, since she was shaking, and probably hurt that her parents saw the change as a waste.

qa.q: What made Gurleen's approach reach her parents better than arguing?
qa.a: A calm opening that named their worry, along with a written plan showing careful thought.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's mother feel about the page?
qa.a: Interested and somewhat reassured, since she asked to keep it, though probably still anxious about security.

grounding: Illustrates a person changing course who meets parental fear and answers it with calm explanation and a written plan.

passage:
Thursday night. Told Papa and Mummy about the teaching course tonight. Papa put down his spoon. "Bank means security. You want to throw it away?" Mummy started crying and asked what people would say. My old self would have shouted. Instead I breathed, went to my room and brought the sheet I made with Rekha didi last week: the fees, eight months of savings, and the date by which I would apply back to banks if it does not work. Papa read it twice and said nothing. Mummy asked, quietly, how much the fee was. I said I know they are scared, and that I am scared too. Nobody agreed, but nobody left the table either. Tomorrow I will show them the school I visited.
Vasudha

qa.q: What did Vasudha bring from the room at the table?
qa.a: Vasudha brought the sheet made with Rekha didi, listing the fees, eight months of savings and the date to apply back to banks.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when Mummy started crying?
qa.a: Scared and torn, holding back the urge to shout.

qa.q: What could Vasudha do tomorrow to keep the conversation going?
qa.a: Show the school Vasudha visited and keep explaining calmly.

qa.q: How might Papa feel about the plan?
qa.a: Worried about security, but reading the sheet twice shows Papa is taking it seriously.

grounding: Illustrates a person changing careers who meets fear about quitting and responds with a calm plan instead of defiance.

passage: When I left the tutoring collective, I promised myself two things: say it honestly, and finish what I had already agreed to. Harsha here. I told Jaya, who runs the collective, that I was leaving because my new job's hours no longer fit, and that nobody had done anything wrong. I asked what was still pending, and we wrote a list: the March workshop, two parent calls and the fee register. I finished all three before my last day. I did not complain about the timetable mess in the group chat, even though I could have. On my last evening Jaya said, "The door is open." A month later a former colleague asked me for a reference, and I said yes without hesitation.

qa.q: What three things did Harsha finish before the last day?
qa.a: Harsha finished the March workshop, two parent calls and the fee register.

qa.q: What did Harsha want the departure to be like?
qa.a: Honest and responsible, with Harsha feeling determined to finish the commitments already made and not blame anyone.

qa.q: Why did Harsha choose not to complain in the group chat?
qa.a: Complaining could burn bridges, and leaving without blame keeps trust and reputation.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel about the way Harsha left?
qa.a: Probably respected and reassured, since Harsha gave an honest reason and Jaya said the door is open.

grounding: Illustrates a person who leaves a role honestly, finishes commitments already made and does not burn bridges.

passage: Head coach's note, Salma. Saurabh told me on the second of the month that he is leaving the club to take a night-shift job, and he gave a month. He explained plainly that the hours no longer worked and blamed nobody. He asked to keep the under-14 team through the district tournament, and did, arriving on time to every session. He wrote a one-page plan for each player and handed the kit list and bus bookings to Devika. On his last day he told the children himself and thanked the parents in person. Two parents asked whether the club had quarrelled, and Saurabh said no, in front of them. I would happily give him a reference.

qa.q: Which team did Saurabh keep through the district tournament?
qa.a: Saurabh kept the under-14 team.

qa.q: What does Saurabh's behaviour suggest he felt toward the children and the club?
qa.a: Saurabh seems to have felt caring and protective toward the children and loyal to the club, since he told the children himself and did not leave them without a plan.

qa.q: What could another person leaving a team copy from Saurabh?
qa.a: State the reason plainly, finish agreed tasks, write a handover and avoid blaming anyone.

qa.q: How might the parents have felt after hearing Saurabh's answer?
qa.a: Reassured that nothing was wrong at the club, since he told them plainly there had been no quarrel.

grounding: Illustrates a person who leaves cleanly by giving notice, finishing commitments, handing over and not blaming, and earns a good reference.

passage: The computer lab smelled of dust and warm plastic. Zubin had thirty minutes before the science project was due and a blank page. "Just this once," he told himself, opening Vijay's file from the shared folder and retyping the paragraphs in his own order. Half the class had done the same last term. He handed it in and felt sick for an hour. On Friday the teacher put both projects on the desk and asked quietly, "Zubin, can you tell me how you reached this conclusion?" He could not explain the second graph. The teacher gave him a fresh topic and three days. Zubin stayed back in the library and, slowly, made the graph himself.

qa.q: How long did Zubin have before the project was due?
qa.a: Zubin had thirty minutes before the project was due.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling after handing the project in?
qa.a: Sick with guilt for an hour, despite telling himself it was just this once.

qa.q: What was the turning point that helped Zubin?
qa.a: When the teacher asked a calm question and he could not explain the graph, he accepted a fresh topic and stayed back to make the graph himself.

qa.q: How might the teacher see the two similar projects?
qa.a: As a sign that a student may be struggling or under pressure, so the teacher asked a calm question and did not punish at once.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who copies work under deadline pressure, tells himself it is just once and cannot explain it later.

passage:
Dear Jeevan,
Last night I finally understood why I am scared of Thursday's test. For three weeks I have been copying the algebra homework from a solutions site an hour before it is due, telling myself it is only for tonight. Everyone in our class does it, so it felt normal. My homework marks are perfect. In class yesterday, Ms Thomas put a similar problem on the board and I froze. I have the copied pages, but nothing in my head. Tonight I opened a fresh notebook and did the first two problems myself, slowly and badly, but they are mine. I am going to ask Ms Thomas for help on Monday. Write back and tell me if you have ever felt this.
Joseph

qa.q: How long before the deadline did Joseph copy the algebra homework?
qa.a: Joseph copied it an hour before it was due.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when the similar problem was put on the board?
qa.a: Frightened and exposed, since the copied pages left nothing Joseph could use.

qa.q: What could Joseph do on Monday and after?
qa.a: Ask Ms Thomas for help and keep solving problems independently, even slowly.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel receiving this letter?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised, but trusted with an honest confession, and likely supportive.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who copies homework each night as a common habit and finds that it weakens the ability to do the work.

subtype: Cutting corners in a group task [Actor]
passage:
Pankaj: Village 5 row is blank. Due in two hours.
Urmila: Only 18 of 30 forms came back there.
Pankaj: Then we write 18 and explain.
Urmila: I will put 27. Everyone pads a number sometimes. It is one cell.
Pankaj: I do not love that.
Urmila: Nobody checks. Sending.
(Next day, 9:10 a.m.)
Pankaj: Sir, our course professor, wants the raw forms for village 5 by tonight.
Urmila: I only have 18. My stomach just dropped.
Pankaj: Tell him before he counts. I will come with you.
Urmila: Okay. It was one cell, but I wish I had left it at 18.

qa.q: How many forms came back from the fifth village?
qa.a: Eighteen of the thirty forms came back.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when Sir asked for the raw forms?
qa.a: Panicked and guilty, since Urmila's stomach dropped and the wish to have left it at 18 shows regret.

qa.q: What could Urmila do after Pankaj's offer?
qa.a: Tell the professor before the forms are counted and correct the figure with an honest explanation.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt about the padded number, then and now?
qa.a: Uneasy at the time, since Pankaj said not loving it, and now supportive, offering to go along.

grounding: Illustrates a student who invents a data point to meet a deadline, excuses it with everyone does it, and faces the consequence.

subtype: Cutting corners in a group task [Actor]
passage: At the small-town college near Sangli, the projector cast the poster onto the wall, and the judge asked, "Who wrote the water-testing method?" Avni had known the question was coming. Ira had spent three nights on that method in the library, and her name was not on the poster; Avni had typed only "submitted by Avni and team". "I led it," Avni said, and told herself that teams do this all the time. The judge nodded. Ira, standing at the back with the sample bottles, looked at the floor and said nothing. On the walk to the bus stand Ira stayed three steps behind. "You could have said my name," she said at last, and Avni had no answer that felt true.

qa.q: What did Ira spend three nights on in the library?
qa.a: Ira spent three nights on the water-testing method.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling on the walk to the bus stand?
qa.a: Guilty and stuck for words, because Avni had no true answer.

qa.q: What could Avni do next to repair things?
qa.a: Tell the judge and organisers that Ira wrote the method, and apologise to Ira.

qa.q: How might Ira feel about being left off the poster?
qa.a: Hurt and overlooked, since she stayed silent and three steps behind.

grounding: Illustrates a student who lets a team member's uncredited work pass as the team's own, softening it with everybody does it.
